title: Which Ram does Kabir sing?
hook: Kabir sings to Ram, but which Ram? Hindus argue it among themselves
carry: saguna and nirguna: god with form, and beyond
tomorrow: a dying poet walks away from the holiest city. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the guru's gift is the name: a weaver took Ram's name from a Hindu guru, and the guru's gift is the name. Today, that same name, argued over inside Hinduism itself.

Two cousins at a family dinner. One keeps a picture of Ram as her phone's lock screen. The other says God can't fit in any picture. The plates go quiet. Kabir sings Ram's name again and again. So which Ram? The prince of Ayodhya, with his bow, his exile and his return? A line credited to Kabir answers, in paraphrase: Dasharath's son is praised through the three worlds, but the secret of Ram's name is something else.
screen: `A LOCK SCREEN, OR NO PICTURE?` → `KABIR SINGS RAM.` → `BUT WHICH RAM?`

segments.voice: Hindu tradition has two words for this argument, and each side has a real case. Saguna means with qualities: God with a form you can picture, Ram with his bow, Krishna with his flute. Its best case is that love needs a face. A God you can see, dress, feed and sing to can be loved the way a person is loved. Tulsidas sings the Ram of Ayodhya, and his Ram has a father, a wife and a long road home. Nirguna means without qualities: God beyond form, beyond any picture. Its best case is that anything you can picture is smaller than God, and the one beyond form is found within, close as the breath. Hindu histories of bhakti place Kabir among the nirguna sants. Both are Hindu ways of loving God, and the argument goes on inside the tradition. Now the never-blended part. When Hindus took Kabir in, they didn't need Islamic doctrine to explain him. They already had a frame of their own: nirguna. A Hindu listener hears Kabir's Ram as the one within, without form. Some Muslim readers hear the same songs in their own frame: one God, beyond every image. Same line, two readings, each from its own house. And inside Hinduism, both stay at home: one family can keep a murti of Ram on the shelf and sing Kabir in the evening.
screen: `SAGUNA: LOVE NEEDS A FACE.` · `NIRGUNA: BEYOND ANY PICTURE.` · `A HINDU FRAME FOR KABIR.` · then, large: `ONE NAME, TWO HOUSES.`

segments.voice: If you have a picture or murti of a deity, look at it for a few breaths: the face, the hands, the color. That's the saguna side. Then close your eyes and stay with what's left when the picture is gone. That's the nirguna side. If you don't pray, use any image you love. Let both belong.
Never blended as doctrine. Here, one name, Ram, heard with form and beyond form, each reading drawn from its own house.
For the road: saguna and nirguna, God with form, and God beyond it. Both are Hindu. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindu devotion holds both saguna bhakti, love of God with form (as in Tulsidas's Ram), and nirguna bhakti, love of God beyond form (as in Kabir's songs); devotees and teachers still discuss how the two fit together.
